name: Sustainable aviation fuels
summary: SAF uses qualified alternative feedstocks or synthetic pathways to reduce aviation fuel lifecycle emissions while working in today’s aircraft within certified blending limits.
useCase: An airline buys a documented SAF blend at a regulated airport, reducing lifecycle fuel emissions without replacing its aircraft fleet.
whyNow: IATA’s production estimates show growth from 0.5 million tonnes in 2023 to 1.0 million in 2024 and 1.9 million in 2025. Its current forecast is 2.4 million tonnes in 2026, still a small fraction of aviation fuel demand. That 2026 number is a forecast, not a completed-year observation. Existing aircraft compatibility helps adoption, but scaling feedstocks and production economically remains difficult. Bio-based SAF and synthetic e-fuels have different resource needs and maturity; combining them into one optimistic growth curve hides those differences. Mandated blend percentages can create demand, yet do not themselves prove that capacity will operate or that airlines will buy more than required.

mainstream.scope: Routine procurement and blending at airports subject to durable SAF requirements and among major airline fuel buyers; SAF remains a minority of total global jet fuel.
mainstream.rationale: Compatibility with existing aircraft and mandated demand support repeat procurement before 2030 in leading markets. The date refers to routine availability and contracting, not majority fuel share. Synthetic SAF is earlier-stage and may scale later; feedstock constraints, price premiums or policy changes can delay adoption.

metric.name: Global SAF production
metric.scope: IATA global sustainable aviation fuel production estimates; bio-based and synthetic pathways combined.
metric.limitations: Historical estimates can be revised. Production is not the same as the total jet-fuel share or lifecycle emissions avoided. The 2026 observation remains a forecast at the October cutoff.
metric.futureNote: IATA’s 2.4 Mt estimate for 2026 is prospective. Longer-term mandate shares are shown separately with their EU-only legal scope; they are not global production forecasts.

milestones.text: No comparable annual production figure retained from the selected recent IATA sources; earlier demonstration activity is not interpolated into a volume series.
No directly verified comparable annual tonnage retained; reported litres and capacity announcements are not mixed into the mass series.
IATA’s later annual comparison estimates global production at 0.5 million tonnes.
IATA reported production of about 1.0 million tonnes, double the 2023 estimate.
IATA’s updated estimate reached 1.9 million tonnes; EU supply requirements started with a 2% SAF share.
IATA expects 2.4 million tonnes for the year. This remains a forecast as of the research cutoff; it is not a full-year actual.

tailwinds: Aircraft and fuel-system compatibility reduces the need to replace the entire fleet.
Fuel requirements and long-term offtake can support financing.
Waste feedstocks and process improvements offer several production pathways.
bottlenecks: Qualified sustainable feedstocks are finite and compete with other uses.
Higher fuel costs limit voluntary demand and put pressure on policy durability.
Synthetic routes need substantial low-emissions power, hydrogen and captured carbon.
watchMetrics: Actual certified tonnes produced and delivered, split by production pathway.
SAF price premium and firm offtake versus uncommitted announced capacity.
Audited lifecycle carbon intensity, feedstock traceability and additionality of synthetic-fuel electricity.
